name: Radu Mihăileanu
teaser: Romanian-French director of humane fables about refugees, train rides, and the stubborn refusal to give up hope at a border.

exploreAction.targetName: Train of Life (1998) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch a village stage its own deportation to survive. Mihăileanu makes tragedy swing like a comedy.

name: Isabel Coixet
teaser: Spanish director who shoots small, quiet stories about longing across languages and distances — often in English, often in winter light.

exploreAction.targetName: The Secret Life of Words (2005) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how two damaged strangers talk around their wounds. Coixet trusts silence more than speeches.

name: Icíar Bollaín
teaser: Spanish director of socially urgent dramas, from domestic abuse to the housing crisis, told through single, unforgettable protagonists.

exploreAction.targetName: Take My Eyes (2003) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the film shows love and control in the same gesture. Bollaín never lets you separate them.

name: Julio Medem
teaser: Basque director of ecstatic, spiral-shaped love stories that wind through landscapes, myths, and twin-like doublings.

exploreAction.targetName: Lovers of the Arctic Circle (1998) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the film spins in circles to tell its love story. Medem's camera moves like the plot does — around and around.

name: Alejandro Amenábar
teaser: Spanish director of elegant, twist-driven films — from a haunted orphanage to a paralyzed composer's inner world — who prizes feeling over gimmick.

exploreAction.targetName: The Others (2001) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how dread is built from fog, keys, and locked rooms. Amenábar scares you with manners, not monsters.

name: Nuri Bilge Ceylan
teaser: Turkish director of long, philosophical films about pride, loneliness, and marriage — landscapes shot like portraits and arguments that run for pages.

exploreAction.targetName: Once Upon a Time in Anatolia (2011) — the first 40 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the night driving scene. Ceylan turns a police search into a meditation on everything — time, memory, men.

name: Zeki Demirkubuz
teaser: Turkish director of spare, punishing films about fate, guilt, and Dostoevsky — he has adapted the Russian master more than once.

exploreAction.targetName: Fate (2001) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how stillness becomes menace. Demirkubuz holds shots long enough for the guilt inside them to surface.

name: Reha Erdem
teaser: Turkish director of dreamlike films where children, horses, and the sea stand in for everything adults won't say.

exploreAction.targetName: Times and Winds (2006) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a village's seasons shape its children. Erdem films wanting with the patience of a weather report.

name: Semih Kaplanoğlu
teaser: Turkish director of the slow, luminous Yusuf trilogy — a boy, then a man, traced through seasons, faith, and memory.

exploreAction.targetName: Egg (2007) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the light on the wheat fields. Kaplanoğlu films waiting the way others film action.

name: Ferzan Özpetek
teaser: Turkish-Italian director of warm ensemble melodramas set in Rome and Istanbul, full of food, friendship, and secrets at the table.

exploreAction.targetName: Hamam (1997) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the bathhouse becomes a character. Özpetek films steam, skin, and gossip like a slow tango.

name: Yavuz Turgul
teaser: Turkish screenwriter-director of crowd-pleasing epics about honor, migration, and the city — his gangster films carry real melancholy.

exploreAction.targetName: Bandit (1996) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a prisoner released after decades meets a country that forgot him. Turgul films the gap between promise and reality.

name: Lukas Moodysson
teaser: Swedish director who jumped from tender ensemble comedies about teens to the brutal poetry of Lilya 4-ever, then back to punk warmth.

exploreAction.targetName: Lilya 4-ever (2002) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how handheld intimacy turns into horror. Moodysson films a girl's fall with a camera that refuses to look away.

name: Ari Folman
teaser: Israeli director who animates memory itself — his Waltz with Bashir reconstructs a war from the dreams and gaps of the soldiers who fought it.

exploreAction.targetName: Waltz with Bashir (2008) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how animation lets memory hide and reveal. Folman draws the past because his characters cannot face it directly.

name: Annemarie Jacir
teaser: Palestinian director of understated road movies and family dramas that map displacement onto intimate, everyday life.

exploreAction.targetName: Wajib (2017) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a father and son deliver wedding invitations through the streets of Nazareth. Every doorstep is a small political essay.

name: Michel Khleifi
teaser: Palestinian-born Belgian director whose lyrical films set intimate family stories against the larger Palestinian memory.

exploreAction.targetName: Wedding in Galilee (1987) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a wedding becomes a negotiation between occupier and occupied. Khleifi films tradition as quiet resistance.

name: Shadi Abdel Salam
teaser: Egyptian director of a single majestic masterpiece, The Mummy, which reimagined ancient Egypt in monumental, almost silent images.

exploreAction.targetName: The Mummy (1969) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the sand and the statues. Abdel Salam shoots antiquity with the gravity of a museum you can walk inside.

name: Mohamed Khan
teaser: Egyptian-Indian director who brought neorealist warmth to Cairo's streets, filming the city's poor with affection and humor.

exploreAction.targetName: The Wife of an Important Man (1988) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how Khan films Cairo like a neighbor, not a tourist. Small apartments, loud streets, real lives.

name: Khairy Beshara
teaser: Egyptian director of lively, politically sharp popular cinema who used thriller and melodrama forms to smuggle social critique.

exploreAction.targetName: Bitter Days, Sweet Nights (1988) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how genre and protest share the frame. Beshara makes a nightclub and a newsroom into political arenas.

name: Merzak Allouache
teaser: Algerian director who has spent four decades filming Algiers — first its youthful rebellions, later its everyday negotiations with the world.

exploreAction.targetName: Bab El-Oued City (1994) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a neighborhood breathes as one character. Allouache films rooftops, stairwells, and loud arguments as civic life.

name: Nacer Khemir
teaser: Tunisian director and storyteller whose desert films are fairytales of calligraphy, wandering, and lost treasure.

exploreAction.targetName: Wanderers of the Desert (1984) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the dunes like paintings. Khemir turns a child's quest into a meditation on beauty and loss.

name: Moufida Tlatli
teaser: Tunisian director and editor whose films give women's inner lives the space cinema rarely allows them — memory, touch, and silence.

exploreAction.targetName: The Silences of the Palace (1994) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the servants' quarters and the palace mirror each other. Tlatli films the hidden labor behind elegance.

name: Raoul Peck
teaser: Haitian-born documentarian and fiction filmmaker who excavates colonial history — Lumumba, the Haitian revolution, James Baldwin — with forensic passion.

exploreAction.targetName: I Am Not Your Negro (2016) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to Baldwin's words over Peck's images. The film argues with the present using the past's own voice.

name: Sarah Maldoror
teaser: Guadeloupean-born pioneer of African cinema whose Sambizanga told the story of Angolan independence through a womans solitary walk.

exploreAction.targetName: Sambizanga (1972) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the political and the domestic share one frame. Maldoror films revolution as it is lived at home.

name: Jean Rouch
teaser: French anthropologist-filmmaker who invented shared anthropology and let his West African collaborators improvise their own stories on camera.

exploreAction.targetName: Moi, un Noir (1958) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the men play themselves and invent their lives. Rouch turned documentary into collective fiction.

name: Marcel LHerbier
teaser: French silent-era modernist who filled his films with abstract sets and Expressionist light, a generation before the avant-garde got famous.

exploreAction.targetName: LArgent (1928) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the machines and the money circulate like blood. LHerbier films capital with the fever of a silent epic.

name: Souleymane Cissé
teaser: Malian director whose blend of griot storytelling and modernist form produced African cinema's first Palme d'Or winner.

exploreAction.targetName: Yeelen (1987) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the light — it's the real protagonist. Cissé shoots a father-son myth in blinding sun and deep shadow.

name: Idrissa Ouédraogo
teaser: Burkinabé director of tender village dramas that showed African rural life with Neorealist warmth and earned Cannes glory.

exploreAction.targetName: Yaaba (1989) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the children's faces. Ouédraogo films friendship and prejudice in a village with a gentle, knowing hand.

name: Gaston Kaboré
teaser: Burkinabé director and film educator who built his country's cinema culture and told stories of children caught between worlds.

exploreAction.targetName: Wend Kuuni (1982) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how silence carries the story of a mute boy. Kaboré films kindness and cruelty in equal, quiet measure.

name: Mahamat-Saleh Haroun
teaser: Chadian director who carries his country's cinema alone — spare dramas of refugees, fathers, and the desert roads between them.

exploreAction.targetName: A Screaming Man (2010) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a pool cleaner's quiet life gets caught in a civil war. Haroun films the war's edge, not its center.

name: Med Hondo
teaser: Mauritanian-born revolutionary who directed searing satires of colonialism and dubbed Hollywood voices — including a famous king's roar.

exploreAction.targetName: West Indies (1979) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch a ship built inside a warehouse become an empire. Hondo stages four centuries of exploitation in one set.

name: Jacques Demy
teaser: French director who painted everyday life in candy colors and had his lovers sing their feelings in full pop-musical form.

exploreAction.targetName: The Umbrellas of Cherbourg (1964) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how every word is sung — even small talk. Demy turns the simplest parting into an aria of regret.

name: Chris Marker
teaser: French essayist of the moving image who invented the photo-essay film and kept tinkering with memory, cats, and the future.

exploreAction.targetName: La Jetée (1962) — end to end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the one moving image in a film made almost entirely of stills. Marker builds a time-travel story out of photographs.

name: Louis Feuillade
teaser: French pioneer whose serial thrillers — an arch-criminal in black, an alluring thief in a catsuit — invented the crime saga on film.

exploreAction.targetName: Les Vampires (1915) — one full episode
exploreAction.instruction: Watch for the proto-superhero energy: masks, traps, chases. A century later, cinema still lives in this serial's shadow.

name: Abel Gance
teaser: French visionary of silent cinema who invented widescreen and triple-screen triptychs for his monumental Napoleon.

exploreAction.targetName: Napoleon (1927) — the final triptych sequence
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how three screens join into one image. Gance wanted cinema to feel like a symphony performed across walls.

name: Jean Epstein
teaser: French theorist-filmmaker who worshipped the close-up and believed cinema's essence was rhythm, texture, and the soul of things.

exploreAction.targetName: The Fall of the House of Usher (1928) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the fog and the faces. Epstein films Poe like a fever dream rendered in light.

name: Fernando Solanas
teaser: Argentine director whose fiery essays and road-movie tangos turned political cinema into poetry and got him banned from his own country.

exploreAction.targetName: The Hour of the Furnaces (1968) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Expect an essay, not a story. Solanas cuts between images, text, and testimony to build an argument you feel in your chest.

name: Jacques Becker
teaser: French director of elegant, humane films about prison, work, and love — he proved that precision and warmth can share a frame.

exploreAction.targetName: Le Trou (1960) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the digging scenes as pure cinema — no dialogue needed. Becker films craft with the suspense of a thriller.

name: Jean Grémillon
teaser: French director prized by cinephiles for films of great formal beauty — the sea, the salt marshes, and the people who work them.

exploreAction.targetName: The Lady of the Camellias (1934) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how Grémillon frames the sea against human longing. He films melodrama with documentary weather.

name: Jacques Rivette
teaser: French New Wave's secret master of the long, labyrinthine film — conspiracies, theater troupes, and running times that reach 13 hours.

exploreAction.targetName: Céline and Julie Go Boating (1974) — the first 40 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the game begin: two women, a strange house, and a story they keep re-entering. Rivette lets playfulness lead.

name: Bertrand Tavernier
teaser: French director and tireless cinephile whose films range from jazz-soaked noir to savage police corruption, always rooting for the underdog.

exploreAction.targetName: Round Midnight (1986) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the music scenes as much as watch them. Tavernier films jazz the way it sounds — late, smoky, and alive.

name: André Téchiné
teaser: French director of delicate, weather-lit dramas about desire and family across generations — the South of France's emotional cartographer.

exploreAction.targetName: Wild Reeds (1994) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how four teenagers' friendships shift with the Algerian war news. Téchiné films adolescence as weather.

name: Olivier Assayas
teaser: French director who films the modern world's textures — global capital, artists, families — with restless, handheld intimacy.

exploreAction.targetName: Summer Hours (2008) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how objects — a vase, a table — carry family memory. Assayas films inheritance as an argument with the past.

name: Leos Carax
teaser: French romantic of the New Extremity who makes operatic, self-destructive love stories — dancing, fire, and cinema itself as characters.

exploreAction.targetName: Holy Motors (2012) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Let the film's rules stay unclear. Carax is less telling a story than conducting a ceremony about performance.

name: Patrice Leconte
teaser: French director of bittersweet romantic comedies and elegant thrillers, equally at home with mime, widows, and a lipstick-red murderess.

exploreAction.targetName: Ridicule (1996) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how wit becomes a weapon at court. Leconte makes verbal dueling feel like swordplay.

name: Cédric Klapisch
teaser: French director of ensemble comedies about young people in Paris, Barcelona, and shared apartments — life advice disguised as romcom.

exploreAction.targetName: L'Auberge Espagnole (2002) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a shared apartment becomes a small Europe. Klapisch films youth as a loud, multilingual collage.

name: Mia Hansen-Løve
teaser: French director of quiet, radiant films about vocation and heartbreak — DJs, philosophers, young women becoming themselves.

exploreAction.targetName: Things to Come (2016) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a philosopher's orderly life loosens. Hansen-Løve films change as a series of small, truthful mornings.

name: Justine Triet
teaser: French director of sharp, unruly dramas about women on trial — literally in Anatomy of a Fall, figuratively in everything she makes.

exploreAction.targetName: Anatomy of a Fall (2023) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a marriage gets dissected in court. Triet turns every domestic detail into evidence.

name: Julia Ducournau
teaser: French body-horror radical whose films — cannibalistic coming-of-age, a driver turned living weapon — won Cannes and rewired the genre.

exploreAction.targetName: Raw (2016) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how appetite becomes the film's engine. Ducournau makes you feel the body as horror and as home.

name: Mathieu Kassovitz
teaser: French director whose La Haine turned the banlieue riot into a black-and-white epic that still defines French cinema's angry decade.

exploreAction.targetName: La Haine (1995) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the long-take opening and the graffiti tag the trio keeps passing. Kassovitz films one night that never cools.

name: Jean-Jacques Beineix
teaser: French director of glossy 1980s cinema du look — neon, obsession, and the diva who sang for a dying boy.

exploreAction.targetName: Diva (1981) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opera-recording heist. Beineix turns a bootleg tape into the year's most stylish chase.

name: Claude Berri
teaser: French director and producer who made beloved adaptations of Pagnol's Provençal novels and bankrolled the New Wave's elders.

exploreAction.targetName: Jean de Florette (1986) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a landscape's water becomes a family feud. Berri films greed with the patience of a farmer.

name: Bertrand Blier
teaser: French provocateur of odd-couple farce — he made Gerard Depardieu and Patrick Dewaere argue, charm, and outdo each other on screen.

exploreAction.targetName: Going Places (1974) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch two drifters live by appetite alone. Blier's anarchic comedy hides real tenderness under the shocks.

name: Renato Castellani
teaser: Italian director of Romeo and Juliet on real Verona streets — a film so fresh it made Shakespeare feel improvised.

exploreAction.targetName: Romeo and Juliet (1954) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the non-professional teen leads against real Renaissance streets. Castellani films the play like a news story.

name: Carlo Lizzani
teaser: Italian director who traced his country's twentieth century — from wartime partisans to the Red Brigades — with a journalist's urgency.

exploreAction.targetName: The Violent Four (1968) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a heist goes wrong in real time. Lizzani builds tension from procedure, not guns.

name: Valerio Zurlini
teaser: Italian director of melancholy youth films and searing war dramas whose visual elegance earned him a small, devoted cult.

exploreAction.targetName: Family Diary (1962) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how two brothers' love is told through memory fragments. Zurlini films loss with a painter's restraint.

name: Florestano Vancini
teaser: Italian director of The Long Night of 1943, a bleak small-town tragedy of fascism that ranks among Italy's harshest political films.

exploreAction.targetName: The Long Night of 1943 (1960) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a town's silence enables atrocity. Vancini films complicity the way Hitchcock filmed suspense.

name: Vittorio De Seta
teaser: Italian documentarian who filmed Sicilian fishermen, miners, and shepherds in gorgeous color — real work, dignified and strange.

exploreAction.targetName: Lu Tempu di li Pisci Spata (1955) — end to end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch an eleven-minute film about swordfish hunting. De Seta makes labor look like ritual and ritual like labor.

name: Pietro Germi
teaser: Italian director who made savage Sicilian satires — the honor-code divorce farce Divorce Italian Style earned him worldwide fame.

exploreAction.targetName: Divorce Italian Style (1961) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a man plans a murder as a social solution. Germi films the comedy of custom with a scalpel.

name: Alberto Lattuada
teaser: Italian director of neorealist tales and gothic comedies — he filmed Lombardy's poor and a bawdy Bell'Antonio with equal gusto.

exploreAction.targetName: The Mill on the Po (1949) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the river dominate the frame. Lattuada films a peasant revolt with the force of weather.

name: Maurice Pialat
teaser: French realist who filmed family cruelty and desire without mercy — a director who believed truth was more important than beauty.

exploreAction.targetName: Loulou (1980) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the rawness of the performances. Pialat lets actors breathe and stumble like real people.

name: Claude Sautet
teaser: French director of quiet adult melodramas — men in bars, old friendships tested by new love — the poet of midlife melancholy.

exploreAction.targetName: The Things of Life (1970) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a crash's aftermath unfolds in memory fragments. Sautet films a life reviewed at the moment it ends.

name: José Luis Garci
teaser: Spanish director of nostalgic, dialogue-rich dramas — his Begin the Beguine became Spain's first Oscar winner for best foreign film.

exploreAction.targetName: Begin the Beguine (1982) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the conversation scenes. Garci builds a whole post-war Spain out of what people say over drinks.

name: Sergio Corbucci
teaser: Italian maestro of the spaghetti western whose Django, a coffin and a machine gun, was darker and wilder than anything Leone dared.

exploreAction.targetName: Django (1966) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the mud, the coffin, and the machine gun. Corbucci makes violence look like a bargain with the devil.
